annotations.text:
1 · The couch bar
Tap the faces — they work on this artboard. Shows that everyone seated is part-way through come first, then ones only some of you are on.
Every card carries the two-part badge: the service on the left, the profile name to pick once you are there on the right.

2 · Finding it
Search is the whole add flow. Each result shows the same service-and-profile badge, so you can see where it will be filed before you tap.
The profile shown is the default you marked for that service. Tap through and you can change it.

3 · Adding it
Who is watching comes from the couch bar. Service comes from the search result. Profile is the default marked for that service on screen 6. Starting episode defaults to the beginning.
The dashed + next to the profile chips adds a new profile without leaving the sheet.

4 · The show
One position, yours. Bump it an episode at a time, or mark a whole season done in one tap when you have been watching without opening the app.
Watched-with is a tag list, not four separate progress counters — the app never claims to know where anyone else is.
The dashed row is the reserved spot for 'leaving the service', which we are not building yet.

5 · Two ways to demote
Not in the mood: half height, dimmed, no artwork, and it comes back on its own after a set time.
Decided not to finish: the smallest row on the screen, still searchable, stays down until you undo it.
Both drop the profile badge on purpose — that is part of taking less space.

6 · Profiles setup
One screen for the profile names as each service actually spells them. Netflix has four, Apple TV+ has two, Prime has one.
Profiles are not linked to people. One per service is marked as the default, and that is the only thing the marking does — it is what the add screen starts on.
The first profile you add to a service becomes its default, so this screen never has to be filled in up front.
Two other directions, deliberately left as rough sketches. Direction A is the one built out on the Screens page. Tell me which parts of B or C you want and I will fold them in.

1 . Ideas
Three sections, ordered by how much guessing each one does.
Ready tonight does none: your own wishlist, crossed with the services you pay for, filtered to the people on the couch. Stalled does none either, and offers a decision rather than a nudge.
Only the third section is a guess, and its heading names the show whose taste it borrowed.
Every guessed row carries three buttons. The heart means we have already seen this and liked it: the show is filed as finished, so it never comes up again and it starts counting towards future suggestions. Thumbs down means no, and is counted alongside the shows you shelved. The plus is the wishlist, for something you have not seen and want to.
The middle row shows what a heart leaves behind. The row dims in place with an undo rather than vanishing, so a mistap is visible and reversible.

2 . Why this one
Every suggestion can be opened to see its reasoning, in plain sentences citing shows by name. One of those sentences is about a heart, which is where the heart's meaning gets explained.
The screen also argues against itself. A similar show you already shelved is listed, because that is worth knowing before committing to three seasons.
The same three outcomes as the row, with words on them. Later pushes it out ninety days instead of voting.

3 . Catching it up
The fast way to vote, and the answer to a cold start. A grid of shows with a heart and a thumbs down on each, so marking ten years of viewing takes about a minute.
Most tiles get no tap at all, which is the point: you are looking for the few you have seen, not answering every one.
A heart files the show as finished without asking for a service, a profile or an episode number, because you are not going to supply those for something you watched in 2019.
The counter at the top is the reason to keep going. Reachable from the cold-start screen and from settings.

4 . What it uses
Each signal is named, counted, and switchable. Your votes are listed first, because they are the only signal you can add on purpose.
The counts come from the real library, so the screen doubles as a summary of what you have recorded.
The second half says what it never reads. That list matters more than the first: the app has no login to any streaming service and cannot get one, which is why its suggestions are worse than Netflix's and also why they are only about you.
Thumbed-down shows are kept, not forgotten, so you can undo a no.

5 . Before it knows you
A new library has nothing to reason from, and the screen says so instead of inventing something.
It still fills the screen honestly. Ready tonight works from day one, because a wishlist entry plus a service you pay for needs no history. The generic list is labelled generic, and now carries the same two votes, so even that block is something you can answer rather than only look at.
The counter gives a reason to start hearting, and the button goes straight to screen 3.
